periods.analysis: The Emergency Response Readiness Score is 86 in 2024-Q3, with no prior quarter in this series for comparison, so we are starting from a yellow but functional baseline below the >=90 target. Harborview’s public health system is not fragile, but the score shows that prevention and response muscle are not yet evenly distributed across all functions. The strongest pieces this quarter were coastal heat-alert messaging, shelter partner lists, and routine medical countermeasure inventory checks at the Bayside Public Health Annex. The watch-item is consistency: after-action documentation from the June harbor smoke tabletop and the West Clinic generator drill was complete, but not yet standardized across every response unit.
periods.recommendations: Keep the quarterly drill calendar in place and add one standardized after-action template for every exercise, beginning with clinics, EMS liaison staff, and the Emergency Operations Center public health desk. Assign Public Health Preparedness to close documentation gaps for the Bayside Annex and West Clinic by the next readiness review. Maintain the working outreach routes for older adults, medically fragile residents, and multilingual households, because prevention depends on reaching people before the event.

periods.analysis: The score remains 86 in 2024-Q4, a delta of 0 from 2024-Q3, so Harborview held steady but did not move closer to the >=90 target. That stability matters during a quarter with respiratory virus season, holiday staffing patterns, and king-tide nuisance flooding, but yellow means we should not confuse adequate readiness with full readiness. Flu clinic operations at North Pier High School and the mobile vaccination unit ran reliably, and the city’s AA-rated financial position allowed overtime coverage without disrupting other prevention services. The watch-item is cross-training: too much of the incident-command knowledge still sits with a small cohort of senior staff on the PH-ICS roster.
periods.recommendations: Continue the respiratory-season playbook and preserve the mobile vaccination routes that reached senior housing, shelters, and large employers. By 2025-Q1, require each incident-command role on the PH-ICS roster to have a named alternate and one completed shift in the Emergency Operations Center. Run a short corrective-action review on the king-tide communications workflow so flood-related public health messaging is faster and more consistent.

periods.analysis: The readiness score rises to 88 in 2025-Q1, up 2 points from 86 in 2024-Q4, which is good movement but still yellow against the >=90 target. The gain reflects practical work: the winter shelter health-screening protocol was rehearsed, the Harborview Medical Reserve Corps completed a 42-volunteer call-down, and pharmacy partner contacts were cleaned up in the countermeasure distribution list. From a population-health perspective, the improvement is most important because it shortens the time between hazard detection and protective action for residents with higher baseline risk. The watch-item is supply rotation, especially PPE and rapid-test lots stored at the Bayside Annex and Fire Station 6 cache room.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the volunteer call-down cadence and repeat it with a weekend scenario, because real emergencies do not follow weekday staffing patterns. Complete a lot-by-lot review of PPE, rapid tests, and oral rehydration supplies before the 2025-Q2 heat and event season. Use the 2-point improvement as a floor, not a finish line, and target the remaining gap to 90 through role alternates, supply rotation, and faster partner notification.

periods.analysis: The score reaches 89 in 2025-Q2, up 1 point from 88 in 2025-Q1, placing Harborview just below the >=90 green threshold. This is the strongest performance in the series so far, and it reflects steady prevention work rather than a one-time surge. The Harborfest medical aid plan, cooling-center activation checklist, and long-term care facility contact verification all improved operational readiness ahead of summer risk. The watch-item is surge communications: the Everbridge public alert test showed better delivery overall, but opt-in rates remain uneven in the South Harbor and Old Cannery neighborhoods.
periods.recommendations: Keep the Harborfest and cooling-center checklists as standing seasonal tools and update them within 10 business days after each activation or exercise. Launch a targeted Everbridge enrollment push through libraries, utility bills, school newsletters, and neighborhood associations in South Harbor and Old Cannery. To cross 90, conduct one joint exercise with Public Health, Fire, Police, Public Works, and two hospital partners focused on a heat-plus-power-outage scenario.

periods.analysis: The score slips to 88 in 2025-Q3, down 1 point from 89 in 2025-Q2, so the city remains yellow and loses a little ground just short of the >=90 target. The decline is manageable, but it is a useful warning because the quarter included wildfire-smoke days, waterfront event coverage, and staff vacation pressure. Cooling centers opened on schedule, and the air-quality messaging reached schools and outdoor employers, but the smoke response after-action review found delays in translating advisories into Vietnamese and Spanish. The watch-item is equity in time-sensitive communication, because a message that arrives late is not preventive care.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the cooling-center operating model and keep the library-community center pairing that worked during the July heat advisory. Pre-translate wildfire-smoke, boil-water, heat, and shelter-in-place templates into the city’s top threshold languages before 2025-Q4. Add translation turnaround time to the readiness dashboard, with a goal that public health advisories are released in English, Spanish, Vietnamese, and Simplified Chinese within the same operational period.

periods.analysis: The score falls to 86 in 2025-Q4, down 2 points from 88 in 2025-Q3, which keeps Harborview in yellow and makes this the clearest signal of readiness drift since the baseline. I am concerned, but not alarmed: core functions stayed intact during respiratory season, yet several supporting systems weakened at the same time. The December clinic continuity drill identified gaps in backup staffing, and the vendor handoff for the inventory platform delayed reconciliation of cache assets PH-CACHE-02 through PH-CACHE-05. The watch-item is administrative readiness, because emergency response depends on mundane things being right before people are under stress.
periods.recommendations: Stabilize the inventory-platform transition by assigning one Public Health logistics lead and one Finance procurement analyst to reconcile PH-CACHE-02 through PH-CACHE-05 within 30 days. Continue the respiratory-virus clinic model, but add a backup staffing pool using trained school nurses, Medical Reserve Corps members, and retired clinical volunteers. Schedule a corrective-action check-in before the end of January so the 2-point decline is treated as a fixable systems issue, not a new normal.

periods.analysis: The score improves to 88 in 2026-Q1, up 2 points from 86 in 2025-Q4, showing that the corrective work is taking hold while Harborview remains yellow below the >=90 target. The inventory reconciliation was substantially completed, backup staffing lists were refreshed, and the February severe-weather tabletop gave department heads a clearer common operating picture. This quarter’s improvement is important because it came from reliability work: cleaner rosters, better cache visibility, and faster escalation paths for vulnerable-population checks. The watch-item is keeping those gains from depending on a few highly engaged managers.
periods.recommendations: Sustain the reconciled cache process by moving PH-CACHE-02 through PH-CACHE-05 to monthly cycle counts with exception reporting. Extend the backup staffing pool into a formal Ready Reserve cohort, with quarterly refresher training and credential checks. To reach 90, run an unannounced call-down and notification drill that measures response time by role, language access need, and partner type.

periods.analysis: The score rises to 89 in 2026-Q2, up 1 point from 88 in 2026-Q1, returning Harborview to the near-green position it held one year ago but still short of the >=90 target. The improvement reflects better execution of the basics: the Ready Reserve cohort completed credential checks, the spring coastal-flood exercise used a single incident action plan, and long-term care facility contacts were verified before heat season. This is a healthy trajectory for a fast-growing city, but growth adds exposure, especially in new multifamily corridors near Harbor Station and East Bluff. The watch-item is scalability: readiness must expand with the population, not merely recover to past performance.
periods.recommendations: Maintain the Ready Reserve cohort, monthly cache counts, and single incident action plan format as standard practice for all public health emergency exercises. Extend preparedness outreach to Harbor Station and East Bluff through property managers, tenant associations, and clinic partners before peak heat and smoke season. Set a concrete next-quarter push to cross 90 by testing surge communications, backup staffing, and vulnerable-resident outreach in one integrated full-scale exercise.

periods.analysis: The latest available readiness score is June's 89, carried forward here and one point short of the 90 target. The Civic Center exercise improved coordination, but its after-action review identified backup staffing at the Bayview pharmacy pod as an unresolved gap; there is no new September score to demonstrate closure.
periods.recommendations: Cross-train the backup dispensing staff, verify the roster in a drill, and obtain the next scored assessment before changing the readiness rating.
